::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Argue that $f$ is not uniformly continuous](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2572729/argue-that-f-is-not-uniformly-continuous), asked by [rover2](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/432062/rover2) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-12-19; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Let $f(x)=x^3$. We want to show that $f$ is not uniformly continuous. [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: TfPF1.png
>
> Can someone please explain from $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)=\big|(n+\frac{1}{n})^3 - n^3)\big| = 3n+\displaystyle\frac{3}{n}$? How does $\big|(n+\frac{1}{n})^3-n^3\big|$ yield $3n+\displaystyle\frac{3}{n}$? ${}{}{}{}$
:::

The first part is just the Binomial Theorem:
$$\left(n + \frac{1}{n}\right)^3 = n^3 + 3 n^2 \cdot \frac{1}{n} + 3 n \frac{1}{n^2} + \frac{1}{n^3} = n^3 + 3n + \frac{3}{n} + \frac{1}{n^3}$$
So
$$\left(n + \frac{1}{n}\right)^3 - n^3 = 3n + \frac{3}{n} + \frac{1}{n^3}$$
The author seems to skip the $\frac{1}{n^3}$ term, but no matter.  The expression is still $>3$, which is the point.
